setup: Start with a problem: how do you tell the story of a people who never told their own? The Celts were a sprawling family of Iron Age peoples across central Europe, bound not by one nation but by related languages, shared art, overlapping gods, and a glory-hungry warrior aristocracy. "Celt" isn't even their word — it's Greek (Keltoi), what the Mediterranean called the peoples north of the Alps. And those Mediterranean outsiders, plus the archaeologists who dig up Celtic objects centuries later, are basically all we have, because the Celts left almost no writing of their own. So this is a civilization reconstructed from the outside, by the people who conquered it. This first chapter starts at the beginning of the surviving record, around 800 BCE in the Austrian Alps, where a community discovered that the rock salt under their feet was, in the ancient world, as good as a gold mine — and built a wealthy, hierarchical, Mediterranean-trading society on top of it. What's at stake is the foundation: salt, iron, wine, and the spectacular burials of the first people we can confidently call Celtic.

bridge: Chapter 1 introduced the Hallstatt Celts — wealthy salt-miners and ironworkers of the Alps and upper Danube who buried their chieftains under huge mounds with wagons, gold, and Greek wine vessels, and whose elite drank imported Mediterranean wine with near-religious devotion. Their art was disciplined and geometric: straight lines, repeating patterns, symmetry. Impressive metalwork, but conventional — easily compared to the geometric traditions of Greece and the Near East. Around 450 BCE, as the old Hallstatt hillforts declined and new centers of power rose further north and west, that all changed. The change announced itself first in the art.
setup: This chapter is about a transformation, and it begins with a single question: why did Celtic art suddenly stop looking like everyone else's? Around the mid-fifth century BCE, geometric order gave way to swirling curves, spirals, faces dissolving into plant tendrils, images that refuse to sit still or hold a single meaning. This is the La Tène style (named for a lake site in Switzerland), and it's one of the great original achievements of ancient art. But the revolution wasn't only decorative. The same period reinvented Celtic material culture top to bottom: twisted gold torcs as the badge of the elite, light two-horse war chariots, near-steel swords, brilliant enamelwork, iron-tired wheels. Driving it is a warrior society where personal reputation is the only currency — men who fought naked, collected enemy heads, and believed the head held the soul. To the Mediterranean it looked terrifying and absurd. It was actually a coherent system, with one fatal flaw built in: it rewarded individual glory, not discipline or coordination.

bridge: By the time of Chapter 2, the Celts had a dazzling material culture — La Tène art, the finest ironwork in Europe, fast war chariots, and a warrior ethos that rewarded aggression above all. But geographically they were still a central European phenomenon, clustered around the Alps and the upper Danube, trading with the Mediterranean rather than threatening it. The warrior system that made them so formidable also made them restless: it produced more glory-hungry young men, landless sons, and ambitious war bands than the heartland could hold. Around 400 BCE, all that pressure found an outlet, and the Celtic world stopped sitting still.
setup: This chapter is about explosion. In roughly a century, Celtic-speaking peoples and their material culture spread from Ireland to central Turkey, from Scotland to Spain — at their peak around 270 BCE covering a range larger than Rome would ever rule. The crucial thing to understand up front: this was not an invasion. There was no Celtic king, no plan, no Alexander directing it. It was organic and chaotic, driven by population pressure, internal rivalry, the lure of rich cities to raid or serve as mercenaries, and a military edge that let them roll over the peoples they met. Gauls poured into the Po Valley of Italy. Others pushed into Britain, the Balkans, and finally — in a mass migration of tens of thousands — through Greece and across into Asia Minor, where one band would settle and become the Galatians (yes, those Galatians, the ones St. Paul wrote to). Watch for the moment a Celtic delegation tells Alexander the Great they fear nothing except the sky falling on their heads. They weren't bluffing.

bridge: Chapter 3 sent the Celts surging outward in every direction — into Italy's Po Valley, the Balkans, Greece, and Asia Minor. Two prongs of that expansion are about to collide with the two most prestigious targets in the Mediterranean world. The Gauls who settled northern Italy, especially the Senones, now sat within striking distance of a still-modest city-state called Rome. And the great migration through Greece, led by a chieftain bearing the title Brennus, was bearing down on the spiritual heart of the Greek world. The expansion that looked like cultural diffusion on a map was, for the people in its path, an existential terror.
setup: This chapter is about two raids that scarred two civilizations for centuries. Around 390 BCE a Celtic army smashed Rome's citizen militia at the river Allia, then sacked and occupied the city itself for seven months — the foundational trauma that, in the Roman imagination, justified everything that came after, right down to the conquest of Gaul. A little over a century later, in 279 BCE, another Brennus drove an army deep into Greece toward Delphi, sanctuary of Apollo's oracle and the richest treasure-house in the Greek world. Both episodes come down to us wrapped in patriotic legend — sacred geese that saved the Capitol, divine earthquakes that crushed the invaders — so part of the work here is separating what plausibly happened from the stories the victims told themselves. And there's a strange afterlife: the Celtic defeats in the east inspired some of the most sympathetic art the ancient world ever made of an enemy.

bridge: The last four chapters have shown the Celts mostly through their enemies' eyes — the salt-rich chieftains the Greeks traded with, the warriors the Romans feared, the war bands that sacked Rome and threatened Delphi. But behind that warrior society stood an institution the soldiers answered to, an intellectual class that held the whole culture together. We've glimpsed them already: the priests who would forbid writing down sacred knowledge, the keepers of a law and religion shared across the entire Celtic world. Now they get their own chapter. The catch is that they're the hardest part of the story to tell, because they made sure of it.
setup: This chapter opens with a warning label. The druids were the most important institution in Celtic society — priests, judges, teachers, astronomers, the carriers of an entire civilization's law, theology, history, and science. And they committed none of it to writing, on principle, entrusting twenty years of learning to memory instead. So everything we know comes from outsiders (often hostile ones, like Caesar), from medieval Irish and Welsh texts written down centuries later by Christian monks, and from archaeology that shows us ritual sites but not what was said at them. It's like reconstructing a university from the accounts of the people who burned it down. What we can recover is striking: a sophisticated lunisolar calendar, the four great seasonal festivals (one of which became Halloween), worship in sacred groves rather than temples, offerings thrown into rivers and bogs, the darker matter of human sacrifice — and a society where women held legal power unthinkable in Greece or Rome. Hold onto that refusal to write things down. It will matter enormously in the final chapter.

bridge: By Chapter 5 the Celts had reached their geographic limit — and Chapter 3's age of explosive expansion was over. They had pushed as far as they could in every direction and were now bumping against powers that pushed back: Rome to the south (which had already crushed the Po Valley Gauls), the Germanic tribes to the north and east, and the Hellenistic kingdoms that had penned the Galatians into central Anatolia. The Celtic world was contracting on the map. But contraction is not the same as decline. In the territory that remained, the descendants of those salt-miners and warriors were doing something genuinely new.
setup: This chapter is about the Celts settling down and building towns. The oppida were fortified settlements of thousands of people — not Mediterranean cities (no grid streets, no marble), but real proto-urban centers with craft quarters, marketplaces, mints, and walls so well engineered that Caesar's siege engineers struggled with them. Manching in Bavaria sprawled across 900 acres. Behind the towns ran an economic transformation: the Celts began minting their own coins (watch the borrowed Greek designs slowly dissolve into pure La Tène abstraction), trade networks carried salt, wine, metal, and glass across the continent, and some Gallic tribes even swapped kings for elected magistrates. Feasting, bards, satire, and pan-tribal councils knit it together. The big question hanging over the whole chapter: the Celts were clearly on a path toward cities, literacy, and statehood — so what would they have become if Rome hadn't been about to cut the experiment short?

bridge: Chapter 6 left the Celts at a turning point: settling into towns, minting coins, building proto-states — but boxed in, with Rome pressing hard from the south. Rome had in fact been conquering Celts for generations already, grinding down the Celtiberians of Spain in wars so brutal that the city of Numantia chose mass suicide over surrender in 133 BCE. The Po Valley Gauls were long since absorbed. Only Gaul itself — the Celtic heartland, divided as always by tribal feuds and never united — remained free. The tribal disunity that had always defined the Celts was about to meet a Roman politician who knew exactly how to exploit it.
setup: This chapter is the conquest of Gaul, and its central irony is that our main source for it is the man who carried it out. In 58 BCE Julius Caesar — ambitious, deep in debt, needing a war to fund his career — arrived as governor and spent eight years conquering an area the size of France, Belgium, and western Germany, killing or enslaving perhaps a million people, and writing it all up in De Bello Gallico as brilliant, self-serving propaganda. He won by playing tribe against tribe. But the Gauls came closer to stopping him than the legend admits. The chapter builds toward Vercingetorix, the young Arvernian chief who finally united the tribes and grasped the one strategy that could beat Rome — refuse pitched battle, burn the land, starve the legions — before it all came down to an extraordinary double ring of siege walls at a hilltop town called Alesia. Watch for the larger stakes: the wealth and army Caesar won here are what he'll use to kill the Roman Republic itself.

bridge: Chapter 7 ended Celtic political independence on the continent: Vercingetorix surrendered at Alesia, Caesar pacified the rest of Gaul with appalling brutality, and an entire heartland became Roman. But conquest of the continent was not the end of the Celtic world. Caesar had twice invaded Britain (in 55 and 54 BCE) without holding it, so across the Channel Celtic tribal kingdoms still ran themselves. And in Ireland and the Scottish Highlands — places Rome's legions could not easily reach — Celtic society would never be conquered at all. This final chapter follows the Celts into that long afterlife.
setup: This chapter is about endings, survivals, and what gets erased. When Rome finally invaded Britain in earnest under Claudius in 43 CE, it provoked the most famous act of Celtic resistance in history: Boudica, queen of the Iceni, flogged and her daughters raped by Roman officials, raised an army that burned London, Colchester, and St. Albans to the ground before the legions destroyed her. At the same time Rome was hunting the druids to extinction, culminating in the massacre on the island of Anglesey — and here the druids' refusal to write (Chapter 5) becomes catastrophe: kill the men who carried the knowledge in their heads, and the knowledge dies with them, beyond any recovery. Yet the culture didn't vanish so much as transform — into Romano-Gallic hybrids, into the surviving Celtic languages of the western fringe, into Irish Brehon law, into Halloween and the Arthurian legends, into the spirals of the Book of Kells. The chapter closes on the haunting counterfactual: what would Europe know if the druids had only written it down?
